entry.title: Generics via Attributes in PHP — Can We Have Them?
entry.content:
tl;dr: How about using generics in PHP attributes?

#[<T>]
class Stack
{
    public function push(#[<T>] mixed $item): void
    {
    }

    public function pop(): #[<T>] mixed
    {
    }
}

Native generics. Will they be in PHP or not? Does PHP need them at all? We'll leave this speculation for the next time, but today let's discuss what generics might look like in PHP attributes.

Status-PHPDoc-quo

Nikita Popov did a comprehensive research on generics in PHP and shared detailed results here. Nikita also wrote a summary on Reddit during an AMA with the PhpStorm team:

The conclusion that Nikita came to is that there are only three ways to implement generics, and none of them will work in PHP. Or rather, it is possible to implement them, but each of them has significant drawbacks.

Nevertheless, the implementation of erased quasi-generics already exists today. I'm talking about PHPDoc annotations.

Although there is no official standard, the popular static analyzers PHPStan and Psalm, as well as PhpStorm, support a syntax that can generally be called well-established.

What prevents people from using generics via annotations? I just posed this question on Twitter. They are, after all, essentially erased generics, pretty much like in Python, for instance.

There were some constructive and substantive concerns raised in the replies:

Nothing stops me from using phpdoc generics, & I use them, but without native language support, I can?t enforce them on downstream users of my libraries, so I still have to write a lot of validation code to check types.

I think this would also be a problem with erased generics.

— Ben Ramsey @ramsey@phpc.social (@ramsey) October 18, 2022

There were also comments about the usability of such generics. But what annoys me, and what the Twitter mob didn't note, is that in modern PHP code you have to use both attributes and PHPDoc annotations simultaneously.

Generics, why no attributes?

The PHPDoc annotations are unstructured strings. They were meant to be replaced by attributes, which are part of the language, and set a strict format for metadata in PHP.

However, in the case of generics, the attributes look terrible:

/** @template T of object */
class Queue
{
    /** @var array<int,T> */
    private array $queue = [];

    /** @param T $item */
    public function add($item): void {}

    /** @return T */
    public function next() {}
}

// The same with current attributes => 

#[Template("T", "object")]
class Queue
{
    #[Type("array<int,T>")] 
    private array $queue = [];

    public function add(#[Type("T")] $item): void {}

    #[Type("T")]
    public function next() {}
}

In addition, the attributes only work on declarations but not on call-site. Consequently, you cannot do this:

/** @var Queue<Person> $personQueue */
$personQueue = new Queue();

// The same with current attributes =>

#[Type("Queue<Person>")]
$personQueue = new Queue();

Generics in attributes syntax RFC

What if generics looked prettier but remained in attributes?

#[<T>]
class Stack
{
    public function push(#[<T>] mixed $item): void
    {
    }

    public function pop(): #[<T>] mixed
    {
    }
}

Pros:

  • PHP code remains untouched and BC breaks are not added
  • The code becomes cleaner and prettier (subjectively)
  • Static analyzers work as with PHPDoc
  • Information about generics is available in the language itself (!)

Cons:

  • Type information still in two places
  • Hacky syntax (?)
  • What else?

Why not all the way native generics with <T>?

Adding native erased generics we get to the inconsistency that some types are not checked at runtime. The attributes never gave a promise to change runtime behavior.

But what about runtime checks?

Since generics information is contained in attributes, it is available at runtime! This means that type checks can be implemented in userland in PHP. Such checks will probably be slower than the native ones, but the main advantage is that they can be entirely optional!

That means you can have early runtime checks in your local and test environments. For production you can disable such runtime checks and get performance boost there.

🚧 Static Analysis PoC

Here is a fork of Nikita's PHP parser that demonstrates this concept. And here is the PHPStan fork with the ability to use this syntax.

What do you think?

  • How do you like this syntax?
  • What problems do you see with this?
  • What are other benefits and drawbacks?


Many thanks to Dave Liddament whose talk at the International PHP Conference in Munich inspired this idea. It literally came up during our discussion after Dave's talk:

It seems PHP generics is a hot topic at the moment. @pronskiy following on from our conversation at IPC, has the syntax #<> been suggested?

Would this work for adding type information for static analysis?

See more in gist: https://t.co/IOzSGgt1Xo

1/n https://t.co/BHkqP3cr07 pic.twitter.com/g2eIzm1ndT

— Dave Liddament (@DaveLiddament) October 30, 2022

entry.title: Turn Any PHP Script into a Native Single-File Binary
entry.content:
For years, I've dreamed of being able to create PHP CLI scripts that can be easily distributed without requiring users to have PHP installed on their machines.

But a scripting language needs an interpreter, they said. Not anymore! PHP still can't be compiled for real, there is a trick you can use.

TL;DR

  • There is a project crazywhalecc/static-php-cli that allows you to compile PHP statically.
  • Under the hood it uses dixyes/phpmicro – it is a special static PHP binary which you can “glue” to any PHP script.
  • What remains is to build the application in PHAR and attach a statically-compiled interpreter binary to it.

Show me the code!

Here's a minimal PoC.

First, let’s download a pre-built phpmicro binary from the static-php-cli website. Since I’m on macOS, I’m using the following link:

curl -O https://dl.static-php.dev/static-php-cli/common/php-8.2.10-micro-macos-aarch64.tar.gz

tar -xvf php-8.2.10-micro-macos-aarch64.tar.gz

Now let’s create a simple application in index.php:

<?php

echo "hello world";

And we are ready to glue it with a PHP binary:

cat ./micro.sfx index.php > indexbin && chmod 0755 ./indexbin

And voilà! Run it:

./indexbin

PoC is nice, but will this work for real CLI applications?

Yes, but there may be challenges.

For a real CLI app, you would most likely need to pack the app in a PHAR file. For this, you'd typically use box-project/box.

I successfully created a basic "hello world" application with this method. You can find it in this repo: github.com/pronskiy/phin

However, when I attempted to integrate something more substantial like symfony/console, I encountered an error:

zend_mm_heap corrupted
Abort trap: 6

It looks fixable, but I haven't looked into exactly what causes it yet.

There will probably be other difficulties with more complex applications.

What about platform support? Linux / macOS / Windows ?

In the PoC above, I just download the phpmicro archive from here: https://dl.static-php.dev/static-php-cli/common/

But for real-world applications, you would want to build it on a CI for all platforms at once.

Micro-php is compatible with the popular Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. Yet, as of now, GitHub Actions doesn't offer free builds for the ARM architecture, like macOS on M1/M2. But alternative CI/CD providers are available, or you could opt for a paid solution.

On a side note, pooling resources in a single repository to fund micro-php builds might be a viable solution. ;-).

Future prospects of this method?

Ideally, all of this can be organized as a ready-made GitHub Action, which you simply add to your repository, and for each release of your CLI-app you will get binaries for all platforms. Users would be able to download and use your CLI binaries without additional dependencies.

Static-php-cli is used in FrankenPHP. Notably, Kevin Dunglas, the author of FrankenPHP, actively contributes to static-php-cli.

entry.title: Running PHP 1.0 in 2024
entry.content:
To celebrate PHP's 29th birthday, I decided to try running PHP 1.0.

So I downloaded the source code, compiled it on my MacBook, wrote a simple CGI server using PHP 8.3, and tried to understand what was PHP 1.0 actually capable of doing. Spoiler alert: not much.

entry.title: The IDE Is Becoming a Token Machine
entry.content:
Or: what software development looks like after coding stops being the bottleneck.

For most of software history, programming looked something like this:

Tiny human.
Big keyboard.
Millions of tiny painful decisions.

You sat in front of a glowing rectangle for eight hours and slowly converted caffeine into syntax.

And because of this, the IDE evolved around one core assumption:

Humans manually produce code.

Everything made sense around that assumption.

Autocomplete helped humans type faster.
Refactorings helped humans avoid mistakes.
Navigation helped humans understand giant codebases.
Syntax highlighting prevented humans from accidentally destroying production with one missing bracket.

The editor was the center of gravity because the editor was where the work happened. And it worked pretty well.

Human brain → Keyboard → Code

Then AI happened

And suddenly the entire equation broke, because tokens became cheap.

Historically, tokens were expensive. Every line of code required attention, memory, effort, frustration, context switching, debugging, emotional damage, 14 Stack Overflow tabs.

Generating 1000 lines of code used to cost actual human life force. Now it costs approximately 42 cents and one prompt.

So the way I see it:

Software development is becoming a token allocation problem.

New world

Human → infinite tokens → slop

The bottleneck moved. For decades, the bottleneck was token generation. Now it is:

  • intent
  • taste
  • knowing what not to build

Code is no longer scarce.

The economics changed

Every generation of developer tooling optimized around the scarcest resource. Early programming optimized around hardware. Later IDEs optimized around human productivity. AI-era tooling optimizes around tokens: the winning systems are the ones that help humans spend and direct more of them.

Most of the debate is about whether AI replaces developers. I find a different question more interesting: what happens to software development itself once intelligence becomes cheap?

Maybe IDEs are not about correctness either

The comfortable answer is that the future IDE exists to keep AI under control. Like a giant safety harness that verifies things, checks the AI and guarantees correctness.

Maybe temporarily. But long term? Probably not.

Humans currently verify AI because humans are still more reliable in certain domains. That advantage may not survive. Eventually AI systems will likely write, test, review and debug code better than humans, and reason across giant systems better than we can.

That leaves an uncomfortable question: if IDEs are no longer about writing, navigating and debugging code, then what are they?

The IDE becomes a token machine

The IDE becomes a machine for converting human intention into deployed software by burning through tokens.

The future IDE probably looks more like TikTok.

Wait what?

Consumer products keep optimizing for immediacy, low friction, instant feedback and infinite interaction loops. AI development tools are drifting the same way, toward throughput and continuous generation.

Old IDEs were books. You sat quietly, concentrated deeply and traversed systems by hand. The loop was slow.

Modern AI tools feel closer to TikTok: fast, addictive, an infinite feed of generated possibilities. Once generating software is nearly instant, the interaction model changes with it.

Eat.
Sleep.
Claude.
Repeat.

The feedback loop compresses so much that building software starts to look like a continuous stream rather than careful drafting.

Maybe we misunderstood programming

Maybe programming was never about writing code. Maybe code was a temporary compression format for human intent, a weird bridge language between imagination ↔ logic ↔ machines.

If so, we are now building a much better compiler for intent itself, and the IDE's job becomes turning human intention into machine execution, as fast and as often as possible.

Once intelligence becomes infrastructure, the most important developer tool is whichever one helps humans direct the most of it.

And economically, the incentives are obvious:

Cloud companies wanted more compute.
Social networks wanted more engagement.
Streaming companies wanted more watch time.

And LLM providers?

They want more token flow.

Not necessarily maliciously.

Economically.

IDE will follow.

entry.title: What 15 years of php‑internals arguments reveal
entry.content:
Not so long ago I left the PHP Foundation and JetBrains. I'm building Omnigraph – it's a graph database for AI agents: typed, branchable, and living in object storage.

But I still love PHP as a programming language, and whenever I can, I keep an eye on what's going on in the community.

For my Laravel Live Japan talk I prepared a Claude plugin/skill that checks previous discussions and helps prototype ideas: github.com/pronskiy/php-src-developer and it works pretty well. Although, not sure anyone except me ever used it for real proposals.

Anyway, with Omnigraph in my hands, I thought: what if I put the whole history of PHP discussions and votes in a knowledge graph? Can this help see hidden and non-obvious patterns there? Can it predict how a vote will go with nothing but the RFC text? Or at least what concerns would potentially be raised? And would it be better than an SQL database + vector index?

So this post is about that.

Who votes on PHP?

In PHP, for any change to make it into the language, it has to go through the RFC process. Anyone can make a proposal as an RFC document and send an email to the php-internals mailing list. Then anyone can speak up in support or criticize it.

After that comes the vote. An RFC's vote can ask several questions; each one is a poll, and the main one, the primary poll, decides whether the RFC passes. About 1,650 people have the right to vote, but in reality usually no more than 100 do.

Who actually votes

Since 2011, 340 people have voted on an RFC, and 100 did in the last 12 months. On a typical RFC of the last 5 years (the median of 357 polls), 26 people vote, and 4 of them stated a position on the list first. Half of all 28,120 votes were cast by 38 people.

This process has existed in PHP and worked successfully for 15 years now.

But even though it obviously works somehow, it also has a bunch of flaws, and lots of people criticize the process. In particular because the vote doesn't always reflect what the community really wants. Although, my research here won't help with knowing what the community wants, I was hoping it could help the community polish their RFCs and reduce chances of getting rejected.

Data model

There are lots of ways to represent knowledge. A graph is one of the most convenient. To represent knowledge in a graph, you need to define an ontology – the entities and the relationships between them. Basically like models and relations in Active Record, except our relations can have types and properties.

With a description like that, we can reliably use LLMs and agents to write knowledge down non-deterministically, but still consistently.

Ideally, you need to be an expert to build a proper ontology, but who am I kidding? With an LLM in hand, I'm an astrophysics expert, a professional doctor and a practicing lawyer all at once.

There are however some good principles for defining ontologies. And I knew that the best ones are already listed in Omnigraph skill. So I took it and asked to build an ontology, and here's what came out for describing the PHP community:

Each box shows how many of them the graph holds.

Agents write everything

Then I vibe-coded agents to pull down the whole mailing list and all the RFCs and write the data down according to this ontology.

Basically extraction is a few prompts that agents run on messages and threads and populate the data in a structured way. It might be efficient to use something like Cloudflare's Clairic, a model built only for extraction, but I used good old (haha) Opus 5.5. So a couple of days and a bazillion tokens later, I had a ready graph of all PHP internals knowledge.

The beauty of agents and ontology is that I don't need to think about how the data will get updated. Each batch of new data lands on a separate branch of the graph, and it joins the main graph only after it fits the schema and I've checked it.

What does the Graph know about PHP Internals?

I asked it all sorts of questions and built visualizations. Here are some examples.

What a bare LLM knows

A bare LLM, asked with no graph at all, recalls the outcome of 100 % of the 2023 polls, 23 % of 2026's and 0 % of those voted after its training cutoff. How individual people voted it almost never knows: at most 0.9 % of votes. Where people stood in the debate it remembers for at most 20 % of those who spoke. The graph holds every outcome, every vote and every position stated on the list.

recalled the outcomerecalled how people votedrecalled where people stood

Ask the graph

How many voters speak up before they vote?

Person ←resolvesTo─ Identity ─castVote→ PollOption ─optionOf→ Poll ─pollOf→ Rfc ←stanceOnRfc─ RfcStance ─rfcStanceIn→ Message ─sentBy→ Identity

About one in seven. Across every closed yes/no vote on a primary poll, 85 % of no votes and 86 % of yes votes came from people who stated no position on that RFC on the list in the year before its vote.

The debate on php.internals is the visible tip. In the 2026 generics vote, 26 of the 36 voters had not stated a position on it before the vote opened. Most of the electorate never shows its hand, which is why a vote is hard to call from the discussion alone.

Do people vote the way they argue?

Identity ←sentBy─ Message ←rfcStanceIn─ RfcStance ─stanceOnRfc→ Rfc ←pollOf─ Poll ←optionOf─ PollOption ←castVote─ Identity

Mostly. Of the people whose first stated position on an RFC was support, 95 % voted yes; of those who first opposed it, 84 % voted no.

The interesting middle is "concerned": people who first voiced concerns voted yes 53 % of the time, a coin flip. Setting conditions leaned yes, at 65 %.

Do minds change before a vote?

Message ←rfcStanceIn─ RfcStance ─stanceOnRfc→ Rfc ←pollOf─ Poll ←optionOf─ PollOption ←castVote─ Identity

Visibly. In 731 cases where someone stated a position on an RFC more than once before its vote, 218 (30 %) ended somewhere other than where they started.

Coming round counts: in 34 cases where someone started opposed or concerned and ended in support, 30 voted yes. Cooling is weaker: in 23 cases going the other way, only 8 voted no.

Sometimes people say so outright, as during the 2026 generics vote:

To my own surprise, I am voting yes on this proposal.
— Levi Morrison
  1. https://wiki.php.net/rfc/bound_erased_generic_types
Queries it ran
bin/internals q rfc_discussion -p rfc=rfc-bound_erased_generic_types
query rfc_discussion($rfc: String) {
    match {
        $r: Rfc { slug: $rfc }
        $s stanceOnRfc $r
        $s rfcStanceIn $m
        $m sentBy $i
        $i resolvesTo $p
        $c assertsRfcStance $s
        $c.status = "active"
    }
    return { $p.slug as person, $p.name as name, $s.position as position, $s.statement as statement, $s.quote as quote, $s.confidence as confidence, $m.sentAt as sentAt, $m.slug as message, $m.url as url }
    order { $m.sentAt, $m.slug }
}
Can you read the vote from the room?

Rfc ←stanceOnRfc─ RfcStance ─rfcStanceIn→ Message ─sentBy→ Identity ─castVote→ PollOption ─optionOf→ Poll ─pollOf→ Rfc

Better than voting history can. Take the people discussing an RFC in the year before its vote, and the share of them against it ("concerned" counting half).

When that share reached a quarter, the RFC got 50 % yes on average, where a guess from each voter's past votes on similar RFCs expected 78 % (25 RFCs). Below a quarter, it got 89 % yes, against 82 % expected (54 RFCs).

I now log a forecast for every new vote before it opens, together with this mood of the list. Once ten have closed, I'll check whether the mood helped.

Is there a fault line in internals?

Person ←resolvesTo─ Identity ─castVote→ PollOption ─optionOf→ Poll ─pollOf→ Rfc

One main line. Put every regular voter (30 or more votes) on a line by how they vote compared with everyone else. This one line explains their votes almost twice as well as any other: at one end, cautious voters who say no more often to contested changes; at the other, change-friendly ones.

It splits close votes. On the 78 contested polls of the last five years (under 80 % yes), 68 of every 100 votes from the change-friendly third were yes, against 33 from the cautious third.

And it is not only about votes: the cautious end also leans toward keeping existing code working when they argue on the list.

Do the people who maintain the code get a bigger say?

Rfc ─touches→ Component ←contributesTo─ Identity ─resolvesTo→ Person ←resolvesTo─ Identity ─castVote→ PollOption ─optionOf→ Poll ─pollOf→ Rfc

Not really. On 767 polls where at least one maintainer of the code the RFC touches voted, maintainers voted yes 3.1 points less often than everyone else on the same polls: a little more cautious, not a bloc.

When maintainers and everyone else split, the outcome followed the maintainers in 34 of 73 cases: a coin flip.

The famous exception is Scalar Type Hints in 2015 [1]. Its 21 maintainers voted 38 % yes against 74 % for everyone else, and it was withdrawn mid-vote at 67 to 34, one yes vote short of two-thirds. The rewritten Scalar Type Declarations went to a vote three weeks later and passed 108 to 48 [2].

  1. https://wiki.php.net/rfc/scalar_type_hints
  2. https://wiki.php.net/rfc/scalar_type_hints_v5

What internals argues about

A position on a principle is a message that takes a side on something general, like type strictness. Backward compatibility comes up most: 17 % of the 38,827 positions the LLM found in list messages. 2015 had the most: 4,715 positions.

Backward compatibilityConsistencyCore vs userlandFormal processPrecedent from other languagesIncremental deliveryError strictnessExplicit over magic

The generics debate as a graph

Everyone who stated a position on Bound-Erased Generic Types before its vote, by their last position, and everyone who voted without stating a position beforehand, linked to how they voted. Hover a dot for the name and their own words; click it for the message.

15 years of asking for async

Async has come up on php.internals every year since 2011: 1,148 messages from 177 people. In 2025, the year of the True Async RFC, async made up 15 % of everything said on the list. Async itself has never had a counted vote: the 2025 True Async vote closed with no votes counted.

Shipped: generators (5.5) · async signals (7.1) · Fibers (8.1) · Polling API (8.6). async/await itself: never.

If we get it right, this could be the most significant feature added to PHP for 10 years or more. If we get it wrong, we might regret it for 20 years.
— Rowan Tommins, on the True Async vote, Nov 2025

How ideas change hands

Failed ideas come back, often in someone else's hands. Of 438 accepted RFCs, 177 (40 %) grew out of an earlier debate on the same idea that their author had taken part in; with the authors shuffled at random it would be 20 %. 59 retry their author's own failed or abandoned RFC (4 % by chance), and 53 carry a failed one someone else wrote, which their author had argued for (7 % by chance). Three of those ideas, and on each arrow the authors of the next attempt who had argued about the one before, or wrote it too:

accepteddeclinedwithdrawn or abandoned

Day one tells the fate

When under a quarter of an RFC's first replies welcomed it, 19 of 43 passed. When three quarters or more did, 62 of 66 passed. Each bar is one RFC: the first thing each person said about it, sorted from the coldest welcome to the warmest.

welcomewelcome with a conditionneutralconcernoppose

Close overall, split on the fight

People who clash on the list don't come from opposite camps. Across all their views, two people in a conflict are no further apart than any two people who argue there. On the subject of their fight, they take opposite sides 47 % of the time, against 28 % for any two.

Hover or tap a dot to see its conflicts; hover a line for what it was about.

Can it predict how a vote will go?

Hard to say. What I managed to vibe-code is an LLM that reads each voter's record from the graph before it predicts: LLM + graph. It predicts better on average than a naive method, but not by much. By the naive method I mean looking only at how each person voted on similar RFCs (knnk-nearest neighbours: find the past RFCs whose text is closest to the new one, and expect each person to vote the way they voted on those.).

LLM + graph against knn on 7 recent RFCs

I tested LLM + graph on 7 RFCs voted after the LLM was trained, so it could not know the results. Each forecast came before the discussion started. LLM + graph got a lower error score than knn on 5 of them (the Brier scoreBrier score: the average squared gap between the forecast chance of a yes vote and the real vote (1 for yes, 0 for no). Lower is better: 0 is perfect, and saying 50/50 every time scores 0.25.). But 7 RFCs are too few to be sure that it is really better.

LLM + graphknn (past votes only)

It's good at copying style, but the essence – not so much

Given someone's record from the graph before an RFC, the LLM wrote the first reply they would likely post (LLM + graph), and was scored on 16 RFC threads it never saw. On whether that reply welcomes the RFC, it did no better than the bare LLM given only the person's name (and the name alone adds nothing: always guessing “won’t welcome” does as well). On who wrote it, as judged by a program that recognises writing style, it clearly did better.

To sum up

Back to the questions I started with:

  • Hidden patterns? Yes. For me, the most interesting was the map of conflicts and principles: people who clash on the list don't come from opposite camps, they only split on what they fight about. And a small group decides a lot: 38 people cast half of all votes.
  • Predict a vote from the RFC text? Barely. LLM + graph beat knn on 5 of 7 RFCs: too few to be sure.
  • Predict the concerns? Not yet. It copies how people write, but their real concerns are not extrapolated well enough. That's what I want to try next, with other approaches on this graph.
  • Better than SQL + a vector index? Not for this data. Opus answered 20 questions about it, once from the SQLite schema and once from the graph schema, and got 19 right both times. What the graph did give me is a review branch for every batch the agents wrote.

While I do have a pool of my own questions for it, I'm also curious about yours. If something comes to mind, write me on X, LinkedIn or by email and I'll try it.
